---
title: "Technology & Differentiation"
subtitle: "Gradient-level detection and correction in a single training pass"
---

## What SART Does

- **Detects** which training samples teach shortcuts — using gradient signatures, not manual labels
- **Corrects** training in real-time — down-weights bad samples and projects out harmful gradient directions
- **No prior knowledge of shortcut types required** — the gradient signal reveals them automatically
- **Plugs into existing pipelines** — works as a training callback, not a pipeline replacement

- Benchmarked against **12 baseline methods** (DRO, IRM, JTT, Focal Loss, etc.)
- **Beats best baseline** on hardest benchmark (Financial-Analysis: +4.2pp robustness over Group DRO)
- **Super-additive synergy**: reweighting + surgery together yield +26.7pp more than the sum of each alone

---

## Why Gradient-Level Is Different

| Existing Approach | Limitation | SART Advantage |
|-------------------|-----------|----------------|
| **Data augmentation / filtering** | Must know shortcuts in advance | Gradient signatures reveal shortcuts automatically |
| **Group DRO / Focal Loss** | Group-level, not per-sample | Per-sample granularity |
| **JTT (train twice)** | Requires two full training passes | Single-pass detection + correction |
| **IRM / invariant learning** | Assumes environment labels exist | No environment labels needed |

::: {.callout-tip}
**One-line pitch:** SART is a blood test for training data — it finds which samples are teaching your model the wrong thing, then fixes the training in real-time.
:::
